_comment: USER-FACING highlights for the release named by `version`, published to the website as
🔴 UPDATE THIS IN THE PR THAT PREPARES A RELEASE, BEFORE TAGGING. The `guard` job fails
the release when `version` does not match the tag, deliberately and as the FIRST job —
so a forgotten update costs nothing but a re-run, rather than publishing last release's
highlights against this release's version. Confidently wrong is worse than absent, and
this file is the one part of the manifest a machine cannot derive.
WRITE FOR SOMEONE DECIDING WHETHER TO UPGRADE, not for someone reading the commit log.
The changelog is already generated from commit subjects and is right there in the release
notes; repeating `fix(events): give payload rows and anchors identities of their own` here
adds nothing. Say what changed for the person running the platform.
Keep it to a handful of lines. This renders in a download menu and a docs banner, not in
a document — a fifteen-item list is a changelog wearing a different hat.
`breaking` drives an automatic warning on the website and in the docs. Set it true when an
upgrade is not a plain `helm upgrade`, and say so in the first highlight.
highlights: A plain helm upgrade from v0.13.x. There is no migration, and no API, topic, permission or configuration key changes — the platform you are running is the same one. This release is about what sits around it: the packages you build against, and the CLI you run it with.

The web runtime is on npm. @devicechain/client, @devicechain/dashboards, @devicechain/widgets and @devicechain/brand are published, so embedding a dashboard or a widget in your own application no longer means building against our source tree. All four move together and are pinned to each other, so one install resolves one version of the set.

Map widgets now expect the host application to provide MapLibre. It is a peer dependency: your app supplies the library, its worker URL and its stylesheet, which is what lets your bundler settle those rather than ours. A map widget with no host configuration above it now renders an explicit notice instead of a blank canvas. This affects you only if you were building our widgets from the source tree; there is nothing to change on the server.
The .NET and Unity client SDK is on nuget.org as DeviceChain.Sdk, built to stay usable under AOT and IL2CPP.

dcctl can now tell you what it has bootstrapped and shut all of it down: `dcctl instances list` shows every instance, the cluster it lives in and whether that cluster is still there, and `dcctl destroy --all` tears down the lot. This closes a real defect — an instance bootstrapped with --kube-context had its cluster guessed from its name at both ends, so destroying it deleted nothing, removed the local state, and reported success while the cluster kept running. Destroy now uses the cluster recorded at bootstrap, and refuses out loud when it cannot.
Dependency and base-image updates across the Go modules and the web console.
